Early detection of cyber assaults is critical, and predictive monitoring can achieve this by identifying unknown attack paths. Previous studies on predictive monitoring have focused on systems for a long time and used a complex method that relies on a large number of measurements, making it impractical for some cyber assaults. Our research introduces a new method that predicts the behavior of a system under attack for a long time with just a small number of measurements. This method works by using model reduction to analyze a large-scale system, and it uses kernel regression to learn the normal behavior and anomalous behavior under attack. Our experiments showing how the method works demonstrate its effectiveness, and they compare our method with others that predict cyber assaults. Our method outperforms others when it comes to some cyber assaults that are highly stealthy. For example, our method detected 90% of cyber assaults that involved a significant amount of data when it used just 25 measurements over a long time, and it outperformed other methods that used the same measurements by at least 10%. Our method also used a processor efficiently, and it outperformed other methods by at least 7.7 times. Our method is effective against cyber assaults that are highly stealthy, and it can detect these cyber assaults for a long time with just a small number of measurements, making it a reliable tool for real-time monitoring of operational technology under

A precise summary can be derived from lengthy written documents via deep learning models, but English language models often benefit from larger training sets and pre-trained tools, whereas summarization for lesser-known Indian languages is hindered by complex syntax and differences in meaning. A proposed model called GAE-ISumm addresses this gap by offering a universal framework that can be applied to any language, leveraging a sentence similarity analyzer and using a greedy algorithm to select the most relevant sentences for a final summary. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this analyzer and the improved quality of summaries generated by GAE-ISumm, outperforming other comparison models including GPT-2 and BERT. Furthermore, the proposed model is showcased through a practical demonstration of its capability to create informative summaries of written documents in the Odia language.

We establish the definition and certain attributes of S-rings of Krull type, in addition to examining the properties of such structures, including upper bounds on the height of the rational subgroups, in correspondence with duality principles for Krull orders, with specific examples and the proof that multiplicative lattices of type A are S-rings of Krull type.

The objective of this study is to understand the presence of unseen binary companions whose gravitational influence causes noticeable star movements in the surrounding area. Researchers have compiled and analyzed data on five isolated stars with documented motions from the 2006 Gaia survey, as well as more recent data from the 2018 and 2019 updates. By applying the dynamical mass calculation method, they sought to determine the most appropriate host masses for each observed star systems. Assuming that the unseen companion plays a major role in their stellar movements, their study used various binary models to calculate the possible mass ranges for the companion objects, as well as their associated epicyclic corrections. The analysis revealed that four out of the five star systems studied have companion masses that are consistent with being within the brown dwarf to super-Jupiter mass range, with one such companion potentially having a mass as low as 1.195 mass units (MU) with a 2.677 MU companion, or as high as 66. MU with a 0.066 MU companion, with an average value falling within the 12-66 MU range, and with an average mass of 24 MU, equivalent to a gas giant planet similar in mass to Jupiter. However, the fifth star, with an estimated mass of 0.81 MU, may not have a significant mass companion, as its star movement may not be as extreme as initially thought. Researchers have also created detailed graphs illustrating the possible mass ranges for companions in six other nearby stars

Recently, Variational Bayesian Autoencoders (VAE), through the framework of deterministic variational inference, have provided a regulatory mechanism for training to achieve well-balanced likelihood and posterior coverage. We offer a comprehensive overview of VAE training under empirical risk minimization. By dissecting the training process into two distinct processes, re-examining the theoretical underpinnings of posterior coverage in light of Bayesian training techniques, and analyzing empirical outcomes, our results reveal that the training dynamics of VAEs are more complex and nuanced than initially thought. Furthermore, our study is complemented by empirical evaluations that examine the effectiveness of stochastic gradient descent in optimizing variational objectives, resulting in a systematic understanding of VAE training. We also present a novel adaptation of the least square VAE (LS-VAE) framework, which is characterized by a combined objective function comprising two distinct components: the standard ELBO and a generalized Jensen-Shannon divergence. LS-VAE is demonstrated to be capable of generating high-quality data samples and achieving better posterior coverage than traditional VAEs on various datasets. We also explore the effectiveness of different regularization techniques in enhancing the performance of LS-VAE.

This concept relies on a private blockchain network managed by the smart home owner, utilizing IoT sensors and devices to track location and time, especially for key items like equipment, medication, and valuables. The proposed system incorporates a private blockchain functioning as a secure key management system, where IoT sensors and devices are represented by distinct tokens on the network.

A novel approach to quantizing log-likelihood ratio storage utilizing deep learning is presented. It was discovered that average L-values of QAM symbols consistently adhere to an ordered relationship, which facilitated the design of a deep autoencoder model. This model was trained on L-value pairs consisting of a 64-QAM alphabet and 256-QAM alphabet, allowing reconstruction of near-original L-values upon input of unknown data. This scheme demonstrated superior performance over traditional scalar quantization, yielding a 50.4% decrease in L-value storage size, 44.2% increase in channel capacity, and 26.3% gain in decoding error reduction. Furthermore, the proposed method was successfully implemented in a practical phase-sensitive receiver for practical phase-relevant QAM signals without compromising performance.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've identified three different versions of the problem, each characterized by a distinct parameter: single-source single-triangle, single-source no-triangle, and no-source triangle-free scenarios. Our findings indicate that using a source parameter rather than a traditional parameter like treewidth yields substantial improvements in algorithmic complexity. In fact, we've developed an algorithm for the single-source single-triangle scenario with a runtime of O(k^2.5n^2.1888) that outperforms existing solutions, including a recently published EXPTIME algorithm. Furthermore, we've developed new polynomial-time algorithms for the single-source no-triangle and no-source triangle-free scenarios with runtime proportions of O(kn^2/(s+n)) and O((k+1)/k* n^2), respectively. These algorithms are based on a new method called "porting," which was inspired by Abello, Kammer and Lee's work on multiseed planarity. We've also discovered that the porting approach can be applied to many similar planarity problems under various parameters. In our analysis, we've identified a new O(n^2) test to assess if a triangle can be ported within another without causing planarity issues, which may have utility in other graph planarity problems as well.

Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. This difficulty is particularly evident in datasets with labels assigned by individuals, a fact highlighted by the poor performance of early works in overcoming noise effectively. This problem's complexity stems from the varying levels of individual reliability, a dynamic largely influenced by personal biases. In light of these issues, we propose a novel ensemble method tailored for overcoming noise in crowdsourced datasets. This approach leverages crowd-sourced label distributions in the form of "human softmax" and views entropy as a reliable measure of annotation noise. This methodology is comprised of three key components: (i) an novel ensemble model architecture capable of estimating noise distribution in human labels; (ii) an adaptation of maximum entropy estimation to accurately assess class probabilities from human softmax distributions; and (iii] a refined version of our approach where the learned noise distribution serves as a soft filter for re-weighting annotations. Extensive experimentation on various datasets, including the noisy Flowers-noisy and ImageNet-Retail datasets, demonstrates the effectiveness of our method in overcoming noise and achieving superior generalization capabilities.

For semiflows with uniformly or nonuniformly expanding dynamics, which exhibit exponential decay in correlations, we can prove the exponential decay in the H\"older norm of the transfer operators acting on smooth observables.

A particular matrix known as a covering array has specific characteristics. It is made up of different symbols and certain sub-matrices must include each combination of those symbols. A particular type of matrix known as a supercovering array has all possible sub-matrices covered by its sub-matrices. If the number of sub-matrices is significantly less than the square of the number of symbols, then it is said to have high structure. In this paper, it is demonstrated that certain types of matrices are highly structured. It is also shown that certain types of matrices with certain sizes do not have a high structure. The former finding resolves a conjecture from another paper, while the latter finding answers a question posed by another author.

This paper examines a unique category of nonlocal games, denoted by $\mathcal{G}_\alpha$, which involve two players using specific types of quantum states when querying two random questions. The paper's primary finding is that if the quantum states employed by the players have a sufficient level of entanglement, then the outcome of these nonlocal games can be accurately calculated given certain predefined constraints on the questions and answers. Importantly, this research sheds light on a long-standing uncertainty principle hypothesis put forth by Connes and Connes in 2016, which states that certain types of quantum data can be easily predicted under specific conditions, and this finding serves as a crucial validation of a lesser stringent version of that hypothesis.

This study partially replicates the work by Soltani et al. who introduced EvoCrash, a tool utilizing a guided genetic algorithm (GA) to efficiently reproduce Java crashes caused by exception handling issues. Initially, the study confirms the effectiveness of EvoCrash in significantly decreasing reproduction time, often taking a fraction of the time compared to a manual approach. Notably, the study reveals that GA's performance degrades when dealing with crashes involving multiple faults, resulting in the production of faulty code that introduces additional errors. Despite these challenges, the study proposes a modified GA variant that addresses the problem of concurrent null pointer exceptions by incorporating nullability information, thus resulting in accurate reproductions of more complex crashes.

The unusual liquid phase, thought to be associated with vortices in high-temperature cuprate superconductors, has been the focus of much debate with proposed connections to both the pseudogap phase and the cuprate phase diagram's various distinct regions. Our study provides new information about the unusual liquid phase by examining its evolution as the magnetic field increases from low values close to the point where superconductivity is lost. We collected data on the unusual liquid phase and found that it transforms from a square lattice pattern to a triangular one as the magnetic field gets stronger, which was supported by numerical simulations. Our research suggests that the square lattice pattern is created when holes accumulate near the material's boundaries, strengthening their magnetic response, and the unusual liquid phase is linked to a state where both electron and hole pockets on the material's Fermi surface are partially filled.

Photons are valuable tools for understanding the properties of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) created in high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions. Recent research at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has demonstrated remarkable precision in measuring thermal photons, and their movement in random patterns has been found to be related to the anisotropic flow coefficients. These coefficients contain information about the anisotropic characteristics of both the initial conditions and the viscous properties of the QGP. A study using state-of-the-art simulations has found that the anisotropic flow of photons is highly sensitive to the way they move within the QGP, and changes very significantly when the speed of photons in the QGP changes for certain patterns of anisotropic flow. This makes anisotropic photon spectra and flow vectors unique tools for precisely understanding the properties of the QGP, and exploring its behavior when photons interact with its complex structure.

Our study centers on investigating the regular magnetic order (RMO) for certain spin models with global spin rotations symmetries in a triangular and kagome lattices. We specifically examine RMO in a global spin-3/2 model, and identify all possible RMO configurations in a kagome and triangular lattices under spin-3/2 model. RMO is found to be stable in regions where the model's parameters satisfy specified conditions, which can potentially be realized in certain frustrated systems involving half-doped manganites and other complex materials featuring kagome and triangular arrangements of magnetic ions.

Large data-driven companies have considered online controlled experiments (A/B Testing) the gold standard for months. A key challenge in analyzing massive experimental datasets at a smaller scale is controlling for false discovery rates (FDR) without overcompensating for correlations within the data. In this research, a more efficient Bayesian approach to detecting treatment effects is proposed, capable of controlling FDR and resisting dependencies within the data. Our method's performance is validated through simultaneous local and Bayesian optimization, yielding highly consistent results. Moreover, we show that the well-known bootstrap method can only control FDR loosely in the presence of dependencies, while generating unneeded conservatism. Our solution instead automatically balances FDR and dependence metrics through an innovative Bayesian pseudo-value statistic. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the most notable results correspond to the most significant interventions, aligning with business priorities. Our method performs seamlessly with standard statistical software and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches including BayesEC, BayesMC, local average and bootstrap in various scenarios, including real-world and synthetic data.

The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are addressed. The derivation of equations governing the inflaton field, an introduction to slow-roll parameters, and a description (with accompanying diagram) of how our Universe emerged from this epoch are presented.

Using experimental data from particle collider experiments, we verify the type-X 2HDM's potential to solve two outstanding anomalies in particle physics data: an electron-like neutrino can potentially address discrepancies with the Standard Model in both muon $g-2$ and the $W$ boson mass. Analyzing lepton flavor universality in lepton interactions, we establish constraints on the new particle's mass and its interaction with other particles below existing mass anomaly limits. Additionally, we explore possible masses and properties of the new particle that could fit recently measured $W$ boson masses.

Software developers who perform maintenance tasks encounter multiple change requests 
submitted by software system users, presenting the difficulty of choosing suitable 
search terms for concept location during maintenance activities. A proposed technique 
QUICKAR leverages the knowledge gathered from the crowd-sourced platform, Stack 
Overflow, to provide reformulated query suggestions based on the relevance of each 
term in the query. By analyzing the co-occurrence of terms in query pairs and their 
individual queries, a model identifies relevant concepts and generates suggestions 
to improve the relevance of search queries. A and NotA are the two classes used to 
evaluate the relevance of search queries before and after reformulation respectively. 
By applying the technique to these queries, the F1 score shows an improvement from 
0.11 to 0.75 indicating significant reformulation results. A thorough evaluation was 
carried out to assess the effectiveness of the technique using 20 queries from change 
request descriptions and comparing the results with a state-of-the-art method.

Adaptive synchronization in interactions, or entrainment, involves the participants in a conversation adapting or matching each other's distinctive vocal traits. To better grasp how people adapt to each other's communication style during conversations, it's necessary to analyze various acoustic characteristics and compare them through multiple measurement tools. This work introduces a novel method, referred to as CENN, an unsupervised conversational entrainment metric, based exclusively on the use of deep neural networks, capable of automatically identifying relationships and patterns in large amounts of data. To develop this metric, researchers examined multiple classification networks, including those using mel-frequency cepstral coefficients, mel-spectrograms, and other inputs, through a series of experiments using a dataset of recorded people discussing topics over the phone. By comparing the results, they found an unsupervised approach using a combination of self-organizing maps, or SOMs, yielded superior performance on a range of classification tasks in conversational speech. To validate this approach, researchers conducted two studies, including one analyzing artificially manipulated conversations and another examining real conversations, demonstrating that the metric accurately captures various aspects of adaptive synchronization in conversations. This work provides evidence of the potential for deep neural networks to enhance our understanding of adaptive synchronization in conversations.

We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data across various astrophysical entities.
These flexible tools enable researchers to create customized visualizations
without requiring users to navigate through a vast array of data, by providing
a simple and intuitive interface to browse and compare different data sets.
Not only do these tools facilitate the exploration of data across different
wavelengths but they also enable users to synthesize data based on user-defined
scenarios, thus simulating various astrophysical events. All these tools are
previously existing open-source projects have been revamped and integrated into
a single platform, allowing for seamless exploration and analysis of data.
Our primary goal is to make these visualizers accessible to as many entities as
possible, including planets, stars, comets, and various celestial bodies, as
well as simulated data, and we're confident that they will serve as a valuable
resource to astronomers and astrophotographers worldwide.

Classifying every video frame into its respective action can be a labor-intensive task, particularly for a large collection of unlabeled videos. Therefore, we present a novel, unsupervised method, called SSCAP, that identifies likely action categories without requiring human annotation, then derives fine-grained, temporal boundaries for those categories without supervision. This framework leverages a novel self-supervised pre-training approach, performing dense temporal correlation check-ups on videos to highlight essential temporal data points, then introducing an action parsing mechanism for joint category detection and boundary determination. To further improve performance, we developed two auxiliary components: one that promotes coherent category associations and another that refines boundaries with commonly observed temporal patterns. Experimental results on JHMDB-21, UCF101-24, and a large-scale dataset called Kinetics SALP have shown SSCAP's robust performance with 73.1%, 44.1%, and 52.1% accurate segmentation, respectively, and particularly its ability to identify category boundaries with minimal supervised data, while also yielding novel, high-quality segmentations using Kinetics SALP as a case study.

We explore the existence of seven hadronic molecular states consisting of $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$, create theoretical diagrams for their production through the $\Lambda_b^0 \to \to \pi^- \Xi_c^{*, \ast}$ to explain their observed mass values, and establish their relative abundance based on production coefficients. Utilizing the current algebra method, our research indicates that the $\pi^- \Xi_c'$ state is primarily responsible for the $P_c(4380)$ state, while $\pi^- \Xi_c^{*}$ is a major contributor to the $P_c(4450)$ state, and that the $K^- \Sigma_c^{*, \ast}$ molecular structures are principal sources for the $P_c(4240)$, $P_c(4280)$, $P_c(4312)$, $P_c(4440)$, $P_c(4455)$ resonances. Our research also examines the decay properties of these proposed molecular states, and our results are further validated by discussing their distinct features.

Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight specific test cases within a program, like those offered by Microsoft's Visual Studio Professional. Nevertheless, studies indicate students are underutilizing these tools, implying there could be learning obstacles related to feedback confusion. To address these potential issues, research has suggested three primary problems related to testing and feedback: limited understanding of proper testing techniques, difficulty identifying effective test cases, and inaccurate execution evaluation. To tackle these problems, three primary solutions of providing learning support, hierarchical test case organization, and high-level execution assessment have been proposed. To experimentally validate these theories, an approach combining inquiry-based and conceptual feedback was employed, offering an alternative to the standard detailed feedback expected by students. This new approach was compared to the traditional method of writing unit tests, with results indicating better performance from students using the alternative method, backed by empirical data and survey responses identifying specific benefits of this approach.

Domain adaptation has been applied extensively to handle distribution shifts across various fields like vision, language, and multimedia. Most existing domain adaptation techniques leverage domain-invariant features by utilizing both source and target domain data. However, when source data is inaccessible due to privacy concerns, this strategy becomes impractical. To resolve this issue, we propose a novel method that adapts source models via hypothesis transfer without requiring access to source data. This approach involves a semi-supervised setting where target domain data is partially annotated. We evaluate our approach with Compressive Sensing-based source models, and the results on two textual domains show that it achieves target performance comparable to supervised adaptations, outperforms other methods significantly, and uses source models adapted with just a few target samples.

A comprehensive analysis of nuclear power systems designed for Deep Space Missions has been conducted, with a focus on Gas Core Reactors as the most suitable nuclear option. Its compactness, high energy output, and moderate temperature cycle make GCR suitable for space applications, and it can potentially utilize uranium isotopes more efficiently than traditional PWRs. In this paper, we examine various GCR configurations, evaluate several thermal-hydraulic and multi-dimensional numerical models, and assess their capabilities in sustaining stable and efficient heat flux extraction up to 10 MW/kg/s. Furthermore, we outline a possible mission scenario in which a nuclear power system of this nature could be employed, and based on that, we calculate the required reactor mass and footprint based on geometry.

This study presents a novel neural network architecture for particle physics research that leverages localization in multi-dimensional time frames. The network architecture is based on theoretical knowledge regarding particle propagation and employs a novel technique to determine time differences with high precision. The results show that this network is capable of delivering accurate and time-sensitive predictions for neutrino interactions, with significant potential in future astroparticle experiments seeking high-precision localization, such as those focusing on double neutrino oscillations or gravitational wave integration with astrophysical data.

The development of models for stellar, substellar, and planetary atmospheres heavily relies on accurate input data, specifically opacities, but various discrepancies persist between existing versatility in methods and the actual implementation, resulting in current shortcomings. Overemphasizing radiative transfer models and thermal equilibrium codes without proper high-level data has limited the progress in these areas. To bridge this gap, we created a database of precise absorption coefficients for H$_2$-and H$_2$O-dominated atmospheres found in brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets across relevant temperature and pressure ranges (10$^2$ K, 10$^{-2}$ bar to 10$^4$ K, 10$^4$ bar). This is named EXOPLINES and is designed for use in future atmospheres work, covering a wide range of species including major lines of H$_2$, H$_2$O, CH$_4$, CO, CO$_2$, and Ammonia, covering 176 lines for these species with associated uncertainties in the range of 10-20%. For calculation purposes, we used the Line List for Precise Spectral Modeling (LLPSM) and made necessary corrections for accuracy. This work serves as a foundation for a larger, more comprehensive EXOPLINES phase, aiming to include and evaluate opacity data from over 400, specifically tailored to atmospheric conditions in the range of 10$^{-6}$ to 10$^{-3}$ bar for key

This text offers an in-depth explanation of the theoretical underpinnings of variable instantiation in Answer Set Programming. We build upon the existing framework of many-valued logic and fuzzy sets, employing them to establish operational semantics for programs with variable instantiation. Furthermore, our analysis examines the relationship between fuzzy sets and traditional logic with two-valued truth sets. Additionally, we investigate how to represent confidence in derivations, focusing on the framework of \calELD-DL.

We have extended quantum resource theories to encompass complex scenarios with multiple intertwined resources like entropy, wholemaking superposition of coherence, and entanglement. A previous study demonstrated that in theories incorporating only relative entropy, the inclusion of a natural transformation is consistent across different approaches. However, we found that applying this transformation to theories involving multiple interlinked resources leads to inconsistencies. To resolve this issue, we formulated a more suitable replacement for the entropy insertion channel using a combination of natural transformations that better align with the resource theoretical framework. We also proved that this new transformation adheres to the first law of thermodynamics for the specific case of entanglement and that it is the unique solution that satisfies several key properties. Furthermore, we applied the generalized transformation to theories involving resources related to coherence and wholemaking superpositions of coherence, showcasing its potential by quantifying the work being done in these environments.

To represent information measures through random variable characteristics, polynomial approximation and best fit approximation are proposed. First, a polynomial representation of Shannon information is expressed via cumulant relations, which are further generalized to non-IID random variables. Next, a best fit approach is suggested, which measures information using optimization principles to match probability distributions with known distributions, and this is applied to modulated sigmodon information measures. Finally, numerical methods and Monte Carlo simulations are used to evaluate and demonstrate the approximations.

We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large sets of time series data, even when individual observations are rare or unusual. A new method allows us to make this analysis without knowing whether certain assumptions hold or adjusting for these potential flaws, resulting in more accurate estimates of these patterns. A simulation shows that our approach can reliably detect these patterns in synthetic data sets, even with significant flaws in certain assumptions. Additionally, we use this method to analyze real data sets related to stock prices and internet data, providing new insights into these systems without making certain underlying assumptions. This method represents an advancement in making meaningful inferences from large data sets, even when underlying assumptions do not hold or are unknown.

A novel set of quantum low-density parity-check codes is introduced, incorporating explicit designs that enable linear time decoding processes. The construction is based on a specific combinatorial structure involving vertices, edges, and faces, defined within a Cayley complex framework. A key aspect of this structure involves an underlying graph that is carefully selected to ensure optimal performance. Specifically, by limiting the code's density and choosing the graph's dimensions wisely, it is possible to ensure that no sparse subgraph of a certain type exceeds a critical threshold in size. Consequently, decoding processes can be efficiently performed, achieving a linear time complexity. Furthermore, the resulting quantum codes exhibit exceptional resilience to erasure, with capacity approaching 1 H-1, regardless of the specific erasure threshold.

The distance-$r$ dominating set problem, focused on graph coverage, has seen progress in finding approximate solutions for specific graph types. This work introduces new constant factor approximations for certain graph structures with specific characteristics, and provides a lower bound on the performance of any algorithm solving this problem for a related graph class. Specifically, it was shown that for graphs with a high number of distinct edges, there is no algorithm that can solve the problem with a better performance guarantee than $O(\sqrt{ln}{ln})$; previously, the only better performance was from a linear programming solution with a performance of approximately 2. And so, for graphs with a high number of distinct edges but also a limited number of vertices, we developed an algorithm that can solve the problem with a performance of approximately 2, improving upon previous methods for these types of graphs. And finally, we were able to show that an algorithm that solves the problem for graphs with a high number of distinct edges by covering clusters of certain size can solve the problem for graphs with a high number of distinct edges by covering clusters of certain size, and that this solution has a performance of approximately 2, improving upon previous methods for these types of graphs.

This research examines the impact of disorder on the correlation between bulk and boundaries in two-dimensional topological insulators of higher order. We explore two specific scenarios: one focusing on the theoretical implementation of the bulk-boundary correspondence for the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological insulator of order two, with implications for real-world systems; and another investigating the disorder-induced transition between $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological insulators and the columnar state. We use a versatile numerical tool to capture the full spectral resolution of localized states in order to demonstrate the disorder-induced transition and to provide a quantitative understanding of the disorder-induced bulk-boundary correspondence, thereby establishing the insulating states' resilience to disorder. Furthermore, we highlight the disorder-induced bulk-boundary correspondence's practical implications on localized state structure, including the disorder-induced bulk-boundary correspondence at finite temperature, using the two-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological insulator of order two as a case study.

Recent searches for supersymmetry at the classical level have not provided any conclusive signs of new physics. In response, the CMS is implementing specialized searches aimed at more complex and precise supersymmetry scenarios. This contribution will focus on three new searches using 13 TeV proton-proton collision data recorded with the CMS: one involving light, universally-composed chargino-neutralino production in events with missing energy and a lone lepton, another with mixed chargino-neutralino compositon in events featuring significant hadronic activity and at least one lon lepton, and a third with mixed chargino-neutralino compositon in events including a hard, separated lepton-lepton pair.

 (1) Light, universally-composed chargino-neutralino pairs in missing energy and a lone lepton events: This analysis targets light charginos decaying into tau particles, with an expected mass below 650 GeV, assuming a mass of 0-300 GeV for the neutralino. It primarily uses events with a lone electron or muon, accompanied by large missing energy and a hard tau candidate. In such events, the tau displays significant hadronic activity and high energy. This new search is performed with the CMS data corresponding to 35.9 fb^-1. The search measures sensitivity to several models, including scenarios of direct production of the next-to-lightest neutralino in its decays into a gravitino. In doing, the CMS is able to set competitive bounds

Novel view synthesis with light field rendering traditionally achieves accurate reproduction of view-dependent phenomena by densely sampling a scene's views, yet these processes are often computationally expensive. In contrast, geometric reconstruction methods only require sparse views but often struggle to replicate non-Lambertian light interactions. Our new model strikes a balance by learning view-dependent effects in four-dimensional light field space and inferring scene geometry using learned sparse volume and density information. Our unique model enables efficient four-dimensional optimization of scene volumes and densities from uncalibrated sub-resolution images, allowing us to accurately handle non-Lambertian light interactions and render more realistic views. Our results show superior performance in the wild with significantly reduced machine learning overhead.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2020 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1288 pairs and 1177 targets. A significant discovery of this study includes identifying 59 novel pairs or subsystems among nearby dwarf stars, primarily, adding to our ongoing speckle program. Our speckle program aims to monitor orbital movements of binaries within the solar neighborhood, specifically, high-order hierarchies, Hipparcos pairs, and also assess 892 members of young moving groups and associations, of which we resolved 103 new pairs.

We are investigating chiral celestial algebras found in celestial holography by using self-dual Yang-Mills theory and self-dual gravity formulated under the light-cone gauge, and also expanding upon the work initially done by Campoleoni and Meruli in terms of the chiral spin connection. Importantly, our expanded work will link the concept of colour-kinematics duality to the idea that subgroups of the rotational symmetry have inherent implications on the structure of the spacetime itself. In particular, this duality will facilitate the identification of the self-dual gravity's celestial analogue with a particular type of integrable system when the rotational symmetry is utilized, and this will lead to the derivation of explicit self-consistency conditions in the context of string theory. These conditions, derived from the previously mentioned duality, will specifically focus on the low-order terms of the celestial analogue of the gravity equation. In general, this analysis will connect the concepts of celestial algebras and the chiral duality to the idea that subgroups of the rotational symmetry have inherent implications on the structure of the spacetime itself.

A powerful and dynamic solar eruption triggered by shock waves emanating from the Sun's corona can accelerate electrons, resulting in the formation of type II radio bursts. Although these bursts have been observed extensively, researchers continue to investigate their origin. To address this, we studied a notable solar eruption on October 16, 2015, that involved an EUV jet, a streamer in white-light, and a radio type II burst observed using LOFAR. The analysis of interplanetary propagation of radio bursts, based on 10-year datasets, identified two sources corresponding to the eruption. The source in question displayed a characteristic "U"-shaped frequency-time distribution with an expansion speed of approximately 1,300 km/s, indicating that the radio emission was generated as low as 1 solar radius above the photosphere. This phenomenon can be attributed to the acceleration of electrons by piston-like shock waves in a developing jet-driven coronal structure. As a result, researchers can utilize metric-type II bursts to monitor coronal dynamics, including the growth of solar jets.

This study introduces a unique, self-contained, functional stochastic differential model aimed at capturing the unpredictable movement of individual vortices within a randomly disturbed, thin layer of fluid. Given that researchers currently lack a comprehensive theoretical framework for their collective behavior, this model represents an important step towards developing an accurate prediction model. The researchers provide an in-depth analysis of how two key variables, mean squared displacement and autocorrelation, change over time. In doing so, they establish a method for determining several essential mathematical constants, which can be verified through computer simulations. This work paves the way for further simulations that investigate the interaction between individual vortices and environmental changes, ultimately expanding our understanding of random vortex dynamics.

The state vector of a boson sampling process can be precisely generated using S single photons passed through beam splitters with M modes. We have found a way to determine one part of the superposed state vector |S, calculating R!(M-R)!/S! terms of the state vector, where R is the number of input photons and S is also the number of input photons. We've developed an algorithm using stochastic sampling to directly compute this part, which also contains quantum information. It has been seen that the calculated part correlates with the entire state vector, specifically their inner product varies between 0.85 and 0.99, which indicates high fidelity. We've analyzed our findings for 4 input photons distributed equally across 6 modes after passing through a specific setup, and for 7 input photons distributed equally across 8 modes after passing through a specific setup, specifically looking at mode couplings, quantum correlation between modes, and entanglement. We've also discussed how the calculated part can be used to determine Renyi entanglement entropy in multi-photon quantum systems.

Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this distribution, conventional methods face significant difficulties such as sparse data scarcity, high dimensionality per time point, and non-independent observations. A new supervised learning approach has been developed to utilize temporal information effectively in such sequences. This approach, referred to as Temporal Dimensionality Reduction for Short Sequences (TDRS), employs a multi-objective optimization that combines a low-dimensional feature extraction algorithm with a classifier, using a multi-task loss function. By jointly optimizing these components, the proposed TDRS method achieves efficient processing and improved performance on simulated and experimental epigenetic profiles, as well as other time series datasets in UCI Machine Learning Repository. In addition, the proposed approach enables comprehensive and transparent analysis of temporal sequences.

Reinforcement learning seeks to develop the most effective strategies through interactions with complex systems, even when the underlying rules are unknown. Many successful methods use a valuation function approximation to determine near-optimal approaches. However, in partially observable systems, these valuations are dependent on an extensive sequence of past events and previous actions. Recent research demonstrates that neural networks specifically designed to approximate these valuations are found to internally calculate a probability distribution of the current system state given its history, or belief. A significant observation emerges that these networks, particularly those using recurrent structures, are able to iteratively refine this belief and use it to make informed decisions. In this study, we aim to harness the capability of these networks to accurately represent and update system states and apply this understanding towards developing new, more efficient observation techniques.

In video action detection, identifying the context contributed by characters other than the subject who performs the action known as the "stalker" is crucial, especially for instances when only a single frame is available. Unfortunately, accurately labeling each frame with precise bounding boxes for all characters in every video is extremely laborious. Therefore, a new approach has been developed which utilizes spot annotations - simplified labels that track individual characters' overall presence throughout the video. These spot annotations are then fed into a combined model consisting of two GCNs (Graph Convolutional Networks) and a C3D (Convolutional 3D) model to develop a context-aware stalker detector. Even using limited spot annotations, this new approach outperforms previous state-of-the-art models, showcasing its efficacy on YouTube Action and JHMDB-21 datasets.

A recent competition, the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, introduced a benchmark dataset to evaluate state-of-the-art image copy detection methods. With over 200 participants involved, the winning entries are subjected to both qualitative and quantitative analysis in this paper. Key distinctions of this benchmark are detailed, including findings on the effectiveness of top approaches, the applicability of different copying techniques, and the impact of varying dataset sizes on method performance.

Our research involves analyzing stochastic processes that are either halted or bounce off the boundary of a given area. These processes' underlying mathematical operators comprise two components: a main, degrading portion that loses its effectiveness at the boundary, specifically in a direction perpendicular to it, along with a smaller, non-degenerate perturbation. Understanding the behavior of such stochastic processes plays a significant role in the stabilization of solutions to associated parabolic equations that incorporate a small parameter. In this context, metastability effects emerge, meaning that, as the size of the perturbation tends toward zero, the solutions' long-term behavior is dependent on the specific time frame considered. Our study encompasses a range of scenarios, including boundary-value problems under both Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. Additionally, we are also investigating periodic homogenization techniques for operators that exhibit degeneracy.

This study focuses on the characteristics of nuclear matter at zero temperature within the influence of intense magnetic fields by applying the lowest order constraint variational (LOCV) method, utilizing the $AV_{18}$ nuclear potential. We discovered that the absence of a magnetic field results in an energy per particle symmetric function in relation to the spin polarization parameter. As a result, we determined that no spin polarization occurs in this condition. Moreover, we identified that the energy per particle is a decreasing function of the magnetic field strength when the spin polarization is absent. We investigated the effects of varying the magnetic field strength on the energy per particle and spin polarization parameters by calculating the energy spectra of the single particle wave functions in a magnetic field. Additionally, we analyzed the effects of magnetic fields on the root mean square matter density, charge density, and spin polarization parameters.

Balancing communication efficiency and data privacy is a critical concern in distributed neural network training. To address this gap, we have created an innovative approach that reconciles the requirements of efficient communication and differential privacy. We integrated Relative Entropy Coding, a highly efficient compression technique, into the distributed training framework. By introducing a simple adjustment to REC, we achieved superior compression with reduced side information. Three distinct quantization schemes - fixed, dynamic, and adaptive quantization - are explored and analyzed in terms of their compression ratios. We have also developed an innovative approach that determines the optimal number of bits for each layer, resulting in improved accuracy and reduced communication bits. The training process involves an optimization algorithm that adjusts the compression ratio for each sample, prioritizing high-error samples. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach can achieve significant communication savings (17.9% in the best case) with minimal impact on accuracy, exceeding previously established bounds by 44%. To further enhance data privacy, we have integrated differential privacy into the distributed training framework using the Optimal Transport mechanism, achieving a high level of privacy at a negligible cost in communication efficiency.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet continuum map of the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex was created using GALEX's near-ultraviolet and far-ultraviolet imaging data, which provided far-ultraviolet imaging of approximately 600 square degrees with an angular resolution of 1 arcsecond. The far-ultraviolet emission from this region was found to be primarily powered by young, massive stars and a large blue loop star, as viewed from the perspective of projection. Two distinct areas of high far-ultraviolet emission, located in the Taurus and Auriga regions, were identified as star formation regions, where dense clouds blocked our view of the stars in first look at FUV Auriga-IV, a region of approximately 150 by 80 arcminutes. FUV Auriga-IV was found to be a large star formation region, approximately 200 parsecs from us, where a large, diffuse cloud was seen to be shaped by the influence of a gradient in background radiation, where the strength of the background radiation, measured in flux, increased from 3 microwatts per square meter, to 7 microwatts per square meter, as the distance to the,scattered cloud, increased from 50 parsecs, to 150 parsecs. The far-ultraviolet emission from this region was found to be a combination of the influence of the,scattered cloud, in the background and an emerging low mass star, however the,scattered cloud,

Structured tables in various documents effectively present complex information by organizing relevant data into a concise format. Current table recognition techniques have been hindered by limitations in available training datasets and the complex layout designs in numerous document types. The inherent suitability of tabular structure to machine learning capabilities, specifically neural networks, has not been extensively leveraged in this context. In response, this paper tackles the table extraction challenge by treating it as a node representation learning problem utilizing Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), where cells are represented as nodes connected by edges corresponding to cell relationships. The proposed approach also employs a novel architecture for GNNs designed to tackle the diversity of layout configurations in documents. Experimental results demonstrate that this method surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions and showcase its effectiveness on a diverse range of document formats.

This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, introduced by Lin and Palfrey (2022), within the context of multi-stage incomplete information games. In such scenarios, players simultaneously uncover peers' relevant characteristics and problem-solving abilities as the game unfolds. Building on this concept, our study provides a complete characterization of the dynamic CH solution for two-person dirty faces games. Notably, our findings indicate that lower-level players determine their characteristics at a slower pace than their higher-level counterparts. Furthermore, our re-examination of the experimental data collected by Bayer and Chan (2007) shows that the dynamic CH solution more effectively explains the observed outcomes compared to the static CH theory.

Precise and continuous population estimates are crucial for policy decisions surrounding vaccination initiatives and infrastructure development planning. As the global population is expected to reach 10 billion by 2030, accurately predicting growth is vital for governments to make informed decisions. Traditional methods, like the national census, are constrained by time intervals typically exceeding ten years. As a result, researchers have been exploring alternative, censuses-interdependent estimation methods. These techniques leverage remotely sensed data, car surveys, and population growth models to predict population growth. A recent study combined the CIES method, utilizing MODIS population density data, with the FCC-derived IMOS dataset in rural Zimbabwe to achieve an average estimation accuracy of 2.6%. This paper adapts and applies the CIES method to Mozambique, incorporating spatial-growth models to improve accuracy by accounting for local trends in rural areas.

Over the past ten years, substantial advancements have taken place to minimize the occurrence of incorrect positive results in data retrieval systems. These developments led to the creation of novel systems such as cuckoo and xor filters. Moreover, adaptive solutions have recently been introduced, enabling the avoidance of potential errors in data queries for specific elements. This research aims to introduce a new type of static filter that eliminates incorrect positive results for negative data sets, showcasing how it can effectively replace current adaptive solutions with minimal performance overhead. The proposed filter has been successfully applied to achieve significant speedup without compromises for a large-scale data retrieval system known as the memory-optimized ball tree.

We've theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between certain laser-induced interactions leads to unique patterns of molecule and spin formation, influenced by both two- and three-body processes. Notably, we found that in certain optical trap environments, stable atom-molecule mixtures and spinized molecules can coexist. Furthermore, we explored the implications of dark states in three-body recombination, revealing that they result in unique patterns of molecule formation that are independent of relative spin alignment. Moreover, in scenarios where spinization occurs, we found that three-body recombination produces molecules with aligned spin orientations.

Accurate modeling of multi-phase fluid-structure interactions requires consideration of complex interactions between fluids and solid structures that mediate intense fluid dynamics. We have developed a multi-scale numerical approach using the smooth particle hydrodynamics method to couple different numerical models for solid structure simulations, such that it can withstand the extreme forces involved in such interactions. We've tested this framework using different configurations of fluid and structure dynamics, and found that it produces accurate results that align with theoretical and experimental predictions, as well as outperforms other methods in terms of efficiency and physical realism when applied to the simulation of ocean dynamics and the interaction of air and sea with a pier.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to a lower asymptotic complexity of $O(N^{3/2}K^{1/2}\log P)$ compared to classical methods.

A recently created TTS model called FastPitch can change pitch, but the quality of the speech made with it gets significantly worse when it's given pitch values far from its original pitch.  In other words, it can only control pitch so much.  We suggest two new algorithms to fix this issue.  First, we came up with a pitch-shifting technique that doesn't change a speaker's unique voice characteristics, which helps make new speech samples sound more natural.  We also developed a training technique where FastPitch is taught to recognize speech with a range of pitches all for the same sentence.  Experimental results show that these algorithms help make FastPitch easier to control.

This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based reasoning challenges in areas like computer vision and intelligent video analysis. We propose a multi-hop reasoning approach, called Hopper, an end-to-end, transformer-based model that makes predictions by sequentially relating objects in different locations and time frames. Hopper's architecture enables it to repeatedly consult the input video features as needed, allowing it to handle complex multi-hop reasoning tasks more efficiently than models that rely on fixed input, such as pre-trained vision transformers. By eliminating the need for expensive attention during initial processing, Hopper significantly reduces computational cost compared to existing multi-hop methods, making it faster and more efficient. Experimental results show that Hopper outperforms previous methods, utilizing significantly fewer hops while still achieving state-of-the-art performance on various video reasoning benchmarks, including TIoU@5 of 87.3% for single-hop reasoning and 90.7% for multi-hop reasoning. The code and pre-trained models for this research have been made available on the link: https://github.com/ruimab/hopper.

Our study investigates lepton-pair production coupled with bottom quarks at the Large Hadron Collider using theoretical predictions from next-to-leading order QCD. The investigation encompasses various factors, including a detailed analysis of predicted outcomes and an estimation of the associated uncertainties based on the dependence on perturbative QCD parameters. Additionally, it involves a comparative evaluation of particle-level and parton-level predictions at the level of approximate next-to-next-to-leading order accuracy, as well as a examination of how the outcomes change when using different methods to account for the effects of colliding particles. Specifically, we are examining the primary distribution of events with identical lepton pairs separated by a specified distance, along with a cut on the mass range of the W boson. The research shows that the uncertainty related to QCD is relatively small, about 0.5%, which could be reduced further by increasing the precision of theoretical predictions through the inclusion of higher-order terms. Since QCD corrections primarily affect predictions through alterations in distance between the centers of mass contributions from virtual particles, which in turn is largely determined by the approximate next-to-next-to-leading order accuracy of tree-level diagrams containing four or more particles, we find that considering the corrections from colliding particle scattering amplitudes in the context of a specific phase space and accounting for the effects of virtual particles on the mass range of the W boson already reduces the uncertainty related to QCD of about 0.5%.
